text.p: The following are the reports carried by Estonia's newspapers on Tuesday. Reuters has not verified these reports and does not vouch for their accuracy:
- The Privatisation Agency held a news conference on the privatisation of infrastructure and announced that the process will not be hastened.
- White-collar trade union TALO agreed to a smaller wage rise than initially demanded at negotiations.
- Mayor of Tallin Jaak Tamm has sued an MP for linking him with corruption in a TV broadcast.
- The foreign ministry demands funds in the 1997 budget to open embassies in Spain and China and a consulate general in Germany.
- The Narva police have arrested a presumed serial killer. Three woman were killed and two injured in Narva in August and September.

- The statement of U.S. Secretary for Defence William Perry was an unpleasant surprise for Estonia, a foreign ministry official said. He claimed Estonia had an agreement with the US on avoiding early statements on exclusion from the enlargement of NATO.
- The fire at Oru peat fields in northeastern Estonia has been nearly extingished, partly due to strong rain yesterday, but work will continue for two days at least.

- Relatives of eight victims of the 'Estonia' ferry disaster have adressed a letter to Swedish Premier Goran Persson and ex-premier Carl Bildt asking him to investigate the eight people, initially and repeatedly reported as survivors but still missing.

- The State Court rejected the appeal of the Royalist Party against the electoral commission , which refused to register their candidates in 1995. Leading party official Kalle Kulbok has announced his intent to give up Estonian citizenship.
- The share ownership of Hansapank in the Savings Bank will drop from from 21 percent to 17.3 percent as the Savings Bank expands its share capital.
- The volume of direct investments to Estonia dropped to 75.6 million kroons in the second quarter as compared to 318.4 million in the first quarter.
- The Finnish-Swedish paint concern Baltic Colour has merged its firms in Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania and plans to seize half of the Baltic paint market.
